meeting_header: Date: 2025-11-18 | Start: 14:00 PST | Duration: 42m | Location: Zoom | Redwood: Alex Rivera (AE), Samir Patel (SE) | NovaApps: Maya Chen, Jordan Lee, Priya Nair, Evan Brooks
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex (AE - Redwood): Great afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, I got Samir from SE.
[00:00:08] Samir (SE - Redwood): Hey all.
[00:00:12] Maya (NovaApps): Hi, Maya here. We are excited — we want a hands-on starter lab.
[00:00:20] Alex: Cool. Today we'll do a focused SDK walkthrough: install, auth, environment config for both Python and TypeScript, and a short demo of the Console and Optimize suggestions. We'll leave time for security questions.
[00:00:35] Jordan: Timeline for pilot — we aim to ship a POC in the next 6 weeks, so this is perfect.
[00:00:42] Samir: Quick note: repo we'll share has two folders, python/ and ts/, and a GitHub Actions example for CI secrets.
[00:00:50] Maya: Perfect. Let's start with Python.
[00:01:03] Samir: Ok, in Python we recommend the package redwood-inference (note: package naming may change), pip install redwood-inference, or pip install -r requirements.txt. Then set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env, e.g. export REDWOOD_API_KEY="sk-...". For local dev we often use a .env and python-dotenv.
[00:01:27] Priya: On the API key, we need to understand rotation and scoping for service accounts.
[00:01:33] Alex: Right — Console -> Teams -> API Keys allows scoped keys by model and route. You can create service keys, rotate, and tie them to a team. We'll share screenshots.
[00:01:47] Maya: Where do we store secrets for CI? We use GitHub Actions and Vault.
[00:01:52] Samir: The starter repo includes a GH Actions job that pulls from repo secrets. For Vault/KMS you can push the redwood key into HashiVault and inject into runner. We also have examples for AWS Parameter Store and GCP Secret Manager.
[00:02:07] Evan (CTO): Any caveats for on-prem or VPC installs?
[00:02:11] Alex: For Private deployments we support a customer-managed control plane; auth can still be via short-lived service tokens backed by your KMS/HSM. We'll send the Private deployment reference sheet.
[00:02:23] Jordan: Can you show the TypeScript flow?
[00:02:30] Samir: Sure. In TS we recommend npm install @redwoodai/inference or the scoped package name — import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwoodai/inference'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); Then client.generate({ model: 'redwood-v1', prompt: '...' }). Note: package IDs vary across registries.
[00:02:55] Maya: Does the TS SDK support streaming?
[00:02:58] Samir: Yes, Node SDK supports streaming with an async iterator; we show examples in the repo. Streaming is a tiny bit different between REST and WS but the SDK abstracts that.
[00:03:12] Alex: We'll also demo the Console quickstart: under Console -> Projects -> Integrations you'll find SDK keys, sample curl, and SDK snippets.
[00:03:22] [00:03:30] (minor crosstalk)
[00:03:38] Samir: Now for environment setup best practices: use separate keys for dev/staging/prod, pin model versions for reproducibility (model: 'redwood-v1@sha256:...'), and use request-level metadata for tracing.
[00:03:58] Priya: We need audit logs for production, who accessed what.
[00:04:02] Alex: Audit logs are available under Console -> Org -> Activity and can be forwarded to your SIEM. We support syslog/CloudWatch export and API hooks.
[00:04:14] Jordan: About Optimize — you mentioned recommendations. How hands-on is that?
[00:04:20] Samir: Optimize surfaces batching/caching suggestions and quantization profiles based on your traffic. Example: for a high token-per-request chat we might suggest small-batch continuous batching and prefix caching for common system prompts. We'll demo the Optimize tab in a sec.
[00:04:38] Maya: Speaking of caching, we tried to implement a KV cache and hit weird errors — maybe misspelled as KV cash in docs.
[00:04:44] Samir: Yeah, sometimes the transcribed docs have typos — it's KV cache. In the repo we include a snippet for storing KV cache in Redis and how to attach the session key.
[00:04:57] Alex: Ok demo time — I'm going to share my screen and show the repo structure.
[00:05:10] [screen share starts]
[00:05:15] Alex: See python/app.py, it reads from .env, constructs client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')). Then generate call below. The sample uses the 'chat' convenience wrapper.
[00:05:32] Jordan: The sample prompt includes user and system messages. Do you recommend message batching?
[00:05:36] Samir: For multi-turn chat, yes — send system once, then stream turns. Batching messages on the server reduces cold KV cache misses.
[00:05:47] Maya: How do we test for latency regressions?
[00:05:50] Alex: The repo includes a pytest load test and a simple k6 script. For more accurate tests we recommend routing traffic to a Dedicated pool or the same region as your infra, and pin the model to avoid call mismatch across rollouts.
[00:06:05] Priya: On SSO — we need SAML and SCIM provisioning.
[00:06:09] Alex: Console supports SAML SSO for orgs and SCIM for user provisioning. There's also RBAC per team with custom roles. We'll attach the SSO setup doc.
[00:06:21] Maya: Any gotchas on SDK versions and breaking changes?
[00:06:25] Samir: We publish changelogs and pin major versions. For CI we recommend installing a specific patch release in requirements.txt or package.json. The Console also has a model compatibility table.
[00:06:38] [00:06:40] (brief pause)
[00:06:50] Samir: Now a quick show of Optimize: this is synthetic data, but you can upload a sample request set and Optimize runs a profile and suggests batching and quantization changes. It will also show estimated cost savings per 100k tokens.
[00:07:08] Evan: If we move to Dedicated, how does auth change?
[00:07:12] Alex: Dedicated uses the same API primitives; the keys are scoped to the Dedicated cluster. For more isolation you can use mTLS between your services and the Dedicated endpoints.
[00:07:26] Maya: Can you run a baseline with our sample payload?
[00:07:29] Samir: Yes — that's one of the next steps. We'll need a representative payload set and expected concurrency.
[00:07:36] Jordan: We'll need test data scrubbed of PII — Priya will own that.
[00:07:40] Priya: Yep.
[00:07:44] Alex: Ok, switching gears: TypeScript example. In ts/src/index.ts we show a small Express route that calls client.generate and returns streaming chunks to the browser. The repo also has an example for Edge Functions.
[00:07:59] Maya: Good. Any notes about bundlers and polyfills?
[00:08:02] Samir: The Node SDK is CommonJS/ESM compatible; front-end bundles should use the light-weight browser client or hit a server-side proxy to keep keys secure.
[00:08:13] Alex: For local env, .env files and gitignored creds are fine. For staging/prod, use secret managers and short-lived tokens. The Console can mint ephemeral session tokens for developer machines.
[00:08:27] Maya: How do we rotate keys in production without downtime?
[00:08:31] Alex: Create a new key, deploy it to your secret store, and then roll in your deployment. The old key can be deprioritized and revoked after verification. The API supports simultaneous active keys for a single principal.
[00:08:44] Evan: Are there per-request metadata headers for tracing?
[00:08:47] Samir: Yes, we support x-redwood-trace-id and it flows to the Console traces. You can correlate to your distributed tracing by sending your trace id.
[00:08:58] Jordan: Let's talk error handling best practices.
[00:09:02] Samir: Retries with exponential backoff for 5xx, but not for 4xx — handle rate-limit 429 with jittered retry. For streaming use a resume token pattern where possible.
[00:09:17] Maya: Any bandwidth limitations?
[00:09:20] Alex: Hosted tiers have rate limits; Dedicated removes noisy neighbor but you still configure autoscaling. We'll share the limit table.
[00:09:30] (short silence)
[00:09:37] Alex: Quick demo of a Python generate call — executing now.
[00:09:45] [demo output: streamed tokens appear, small pause, then full response]
[00:10:00] Maya: Looks good. Latency seems fine on this sample.
[00:10:05] Samir: Reminder: local dev hits hosted endpoint by default; for Private you'll point to your VPC endpoint and set REDWOOD_ENDPOINT in env.
[00:10:18] Priya: Security question: do you support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest?
[00:10:22] Alex: Yes — for Private and Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key wrapping and secrets. We also support bringing your own key for S3 buckets used in certain workflows.
[00:10:35] Jordan: What about data retention and deletion APIs?
[00:10:38] Alex: We have data retention controls per project and deletion APIs to purge logs and training data; we will include the retention SLA doc.
[00:10:48] Maya: Anything about multi-region traffic? We need APAC region.
[00:10:52] Samir: We have hosted regions in NA/EMEA and expanding APAC; you can route by region and set failover. For multi-region consistency we recommend model pinning across regions.
[00:11:06] Alex: Ok heading toward wrap — recap next steps.
[00:11:10] [11:10 marker — meeting hits Q&A portion; timestamps less frequent as dialog speeds up]
[00:11:20] Priya: Can you email SOC2 + ISO docs and the SSO playbook?
[00:11:24] Alex: Yes, will attach to the follow-up email.
[00:11:27] Maya: Send the starter repo link so we can fork and run.
[00:11:30] Alex: On it.
[00:11:33] Evan: We'll follow up to schedule the performance baseline.
[00:11:36] Samir: I'll propose times.
[00:11:39] [wrap up small talk]
[00:11:50] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll send the repo, security packet, and sample test harness.
[00:11:56] Maya: Thanks.
[00:12:00] [meeting ends — note: recording truncated in transcript; final minutes summarized]

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., 'KV cash', 'samal' for SAML). Code sample references the starter repo; link is shared post-call. Action items and next steps captured separately.
